VBO:0200376.summary: Friendly and active, Rough Collies often pair an easy sociability with a watchful interest in what is happening around them. They descend from the working dogs of Scottish shepherds, and many retain the ability to herd when given the chance. Rough and Smooth Collies share that recent ancestry despite their very different coats.
VBO:0200376.historicalRoots: Scottish shepherding collie, refined in Great Britain.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 156: Collie (Rough)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 156 describes friendly, happy, active temperament, a quick alert look when listening, Scottish shepherd working ancestry, shared recent Rough/Smooth ancestry despite coat length, and many dogs still capable of work; it also describes the low-carried tail, tipped ears, abundant mane and sable/white markings.

VBO:0200948.summary: The Norrbottenspets is often lively, alert and quick to use its voice when something catches its attention. This bold but kindly northern hunter is especially associated with barking at forest birds in trees. The breed survived on remote Swedish homesteads after it had been declared extinct.
VBO:0200948.historicalRoots: Northern Swedish hunting spitz, preserved on Norrbotten homesteads.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 276: Norrbottenspets
sources.evidence: FCI No. 276 identifies an attentive, bold, lively hunting spitz with kind disposition; forest grouse hunting, homestead survival and explicit small slightly rectangular build; it describes erect ears, a high loose tail curve and white coat with red/yellow patches.

sources.title: Swedish Kennel Club: Norrbottenspets
sources.evidence: SKK describes rapid alert response that is often vocal, tree-barking forest-bird hunting and the rediscovery of the breed on northern homesteads after it was declared extinct.

VBO:0201293.summary: Stabijhouns often combine affection with an independent streak; at home they can be quiet and watchful, while unfamiliar people may meet a reserved first response. Their Frisian farm history is unusually varied: they pointed game, guarded yards and caught moles and polecats, with smaller dogs once carried by bicycle to reach more trapping ground.
VBO:0201293.historicalRoots: Versatile pointing and farm dog from the Frisian forest area of the Netherlands.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 222: Stabijhoun
sources.evidence: The standard describes affection, independence, headstrong tendencies, quiet vigilance and initial reserve; historic pointing, yard guarding, mole/polecat catching and bicycle transport; functional slightly long build, black-and-white coat, moderate feathering and low bushy tail.

VBO:0200145.summary: Groenendaels often show the Belgian Shepherd’s watchful, energetic character and a strong attachment to their people. They were developed from Belgium’s herding dogs to mind flocks and guard property, work that rewards alertness and quick shifts into action. Their long black coat identifies one of four varieties recognized within the same working breed.
VBO:0200145.historicalRoots: Belgian herding and guarding dog, organized as one breed in the 1890s.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 15: Belgian Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: Shared Belgian Shepherd behavior is watchful, active, energetic, confident and ready for action; historical utilization includes herding, guarding and service work. Groenendael is the long-haired uniform-black variety.

sources.title: AKC: Belgian Sheepdog
sources.evidence: AKC describes the Groenendael/Belgian Sheepdog as a hard-working herder with strong desire for human company; used only to support people attachment, not a difference from other Belgian varieties.

VBO:0200347.summary: Powder Puff Chinese Cresteds tend to be affectionate companions with a playful, alert streak. They often seek out a high perch to watch the room and enjoy staying close to their people; some channel that liveliness into agility. The fully coated Powder Puff and Hairless are two varieties of the same breed.
VBO:0200347.historicalRoots: Coated variety of the Chinese Crested companion breed; precise early geographic origin remains uncertain.

sources.title: Chinese Crested Club of America: The Chinese Crested
sources.evidence: Parent breed club identifies Hairless and Powderpuff varieties and describes shared alert, people-oriented, playful/comic habits, liking high perches, and interest in performance activities. It does not claim a temperament difference between coat varieties.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 288: Chinese Crested Dog
sources.evidence: FCI recognizes Hairless and Powder Puff varieties, describes the Powder Puff as fully covered by a long soft veil coat, and calls the breed happy; it explicitly says precise origin is difficult to pinpoint.

sources.title: AKC Chinese Crested breed standard
sources.evidence: AKC identifies Powderpuff as a fully coated variety with straight soft double coat; breed temperament is gay and alert.

VBO:0200377.summary: Outgoing and quick to learn, Smooth Collies tend to form close bonds with their families and respond well to patient, reward-based training. They may bark at an unfamiliar sound but usually settle when a visitor is welcomed, showing the alert yet steady manner valued in this British sheepdog.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 296: Collie Smooth
sources.evidence: Friendly temperament without nervousness or aggression; sheepdog role, alert expression, effortless movement and short flat harsh double coat.

sources.title: Smooth Collie Club of Great Britain: About the Smooth Collie
sources.evidence: Breed club describes outgoing, friendly, quick-learning temperament, close family bonds, response to reward-based training, alert barking at unfamiliar sounds, and settling with invited visitors.

VBO:0200956.summary: Brave and energetic on a hunt, the Black Norwegian Elkhound works close to its handler and is valued for quiet cooperation. In Norway it tracks elk and deer on a lead, staying calm near game so the hunter can approach; away from work, the breed is known for a devoted bond with its family.
VBO:0200956.historicalRoots: Norwegian black elkhound specialized for leashed big-game tracking.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 268: Norwegian Elkhound Black
sources.evidence: FCI calls it fearless, brave, energetic and an elk hunter. NKK documents leashed elk/deer tracking, close cooperation, quiet behavior near game and family attachment.

sources.title: Norwegian Kennel Club: Norsk elghund sort
sources.evidence: Leashed elk/deer work; quiet close cooperation with handler; affectionate family bond.

VBO:0200700.summary: Friendly and high-spirited, the Irish Red and White Setter brings determination and courage to field work. It was bred chiefly as a working setter; after the solid-red Irish Setter became more prominent, supporters revived this distinct red-and-white breed during the twentieth century.
VBO:0200700.historicalRoots: Older Irish field-setting type revived during the twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 330: Irish Red and White Setter
sources.evidence: FCI specifies chiefly field use, keen friendly determined courageous character, older ancestry than solid-red Setter and 1920s revival.

VBO:0200880.summary: Devoted and energetic, the Miniature American Shepherd tends to be watchful with strangers and eager to work with familiar people. Developed from smaller Australian Shepherds in California, it kept a strong herding instinct and approaches tasks with persistence and lively attention.
VBO:0200880.historicalRoots: Developed in California from smaller Australian Shepherds for ranch work.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 367: Miniature American Shepherd
sources.evidence: FCI documents California 1960s development from small Australian Shepherds, alert energetic persistent devoted character, reserve with strangers, and sheep/goat herding.

VBO:0201084.summary: Prague Ratters are often gentle and affectionate with familiar people, curious about their surroundings and a little reserved with strangers. Their lively quickness recalls an earlier role catching rats, while their history also reaches the courts of Bohemian rulers.
VBO:0201084.historicalRoots: Czech rat-catching and royal-court companion history

sources.title: FCI standard No. 363: Prague Ratter
sources.evidence: FCI No. 363 describes gentle, curious, affectionate behavior, slight reserve with strangers, lively quick movement, former rat killing, and historic presence at Bohemian royal courts.

VBO:0200275.summary: Canadian Eskimo Dogs can be quietly affectionate and curious with people, while group-raised dogs often show strong pack relationships. Their powerful response to work reflects centuries alongside Inuit communities as sled and pack dogs; they also helped hunters locate seal breathing holes.
VBO:0200275.historicalRoots: Inuit Arctic transport and hunting partner in Canada

sources.title: FCI standard No. 211: Canadian Eskimo Dog
sources.evidence: FCI No. 211 describes gentle affection and quiet curiosity, structured pack relationships, strong response to work, Inuit history and sled, pack and seal-hunting tasks.

VBO:0200499.summary: Alert and distinctly terrier-like, the English Toy Terrier tends to meet the world with quick attention without being unduly nervous. That alertness has a working history: earlier dogs performed in rat pits, a demanding task behind this small breed’s confident presence.
VBO:0200499.historicalRoots: British toy terrier with historic rat-pit work

sources.title: FCI standard No. 13: English Toy Terrier (Black & Tan)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 13 calls the breed alert, toy-sized with terrier characteristics, never unduly nervous, and records historic rat-pit performance.

VBO:0200704.summary: Irish Terriers are often loyal and affectionate with people, yet ready to stand their ground when challenged. Their courage carried them beyond the farmyard: after working as hunters and guards, they served as messengers amid the noise and confusion of First World War trenches.
VBO:0200704.historicalRoots: Irish farm, guard and hunting terrier; First World War messenger

sources.title: FCI standard No. 139: Irish Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI No. 139 describes loyalty, good temper and affection toward people, courage when attacked, versatile farmyard/guard/hunting roles, and First World War messenger service.

VBO:0200765.summary: King Charles Spaniels tend to be gentle and affectionate, with a happy side that can sit alongside reserve around unfamiliar people. Long prized as companions in England, these toy spaniels took their name from the dogs favored by King Charles II. Their history began with smaller spaniels related to gun dogs, even though companionship became their defining role.
VBO:0200765.historicalRoots: English toy companion, historically favored by King Charles II

sources.title: FCI standard No. 128: King Charles Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI No. 128 describes happy, gentle, affectionate and reserved temperament, long English companion history, King Charles II naming, and descent from smaller setter-type dogs.

VBO:0200987.summary: Parson Russell Terriers are often confident, energetic and friendly, with the boldness of a dog bred to work below ground. Their fox-working history explains the breed’s agile, persistent style. The name honors the Reverend John Russell, whose Victorian hunting terriers shaped the strain later recognized as a separate breed.
VBO:0200987.historicalRoots: British fox-working terrier associated with Reverend John Russell

sources.title: FCI standard No. 339: Parson Russell Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI No. 339 describes confident, energetic, happy, bold and friendly temperament, fox work and ability to go to ground, and the Reverend John Russell origin.

VBO:0200807.summary: Lakelands tend to be bold, friendly and self-confident, quick to notice what happens around them. Their lively expectation has a practical history: farmers in England’s Lake District developed these terriers to pursue foxes that threatened sheep across the rocky fells.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 70: Lakeland Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI No. 70 describes fearless, keen, quick-moving, bold, friendly and self-confident temperament; AKC breed history identifies Lake District farmers and work against sheep-stealing foxes.

sources.title: American Kennel Club: Lakeland Terrier
sources.evidence: AKC describes origin in the English Lake District and pack work against foxes that threatened sheep.

VBO:0200146.summary: Laekenois often show the Belgian Shepherd’s watchful, energetic readiness to act. Their farm ancestors shifted between moving flocks and guarding property, work that prizes close attention to a person and quick responses. The Laeken name ties this variety to a Belgian district near Brussels.
VBO:0200146.historicalRoots: Belgian herding and guarding tradition, organized as a breed in the 1890s.

sources.title: FCI: Belgian Shepherd Dog (Standard No. 15)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 15 documents watchful, active, energetic temperament; original sheepdog use and later guarding and service work. It names Laekenois as rough-haired, one of four coat varieties.

sources.title: AKC: Belgian Laekenois
sources.evidence: AKC states Laekenois resembles its three Belgian relatives in body and temperament and differs by coat and regional origin.

VBO:0200147.summary: Malinois tend to be intensely alert working partners with a strong attachment to their people. On small Belgian farms, dogs of this line moved mixed livestock and watched boundaries without fences. That blend of attention and stamina later found a place in tracking, scent detection and service work.
VBO:0200147.historicalRoots: Belgian farm herder associated with Mechelen; later versatile service and detection work.

sources.title: FCI: Belgian Shepherd Dog (Standard No. 15)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 15 describes shared Belgian Shepherd vigilance, energy, herding, guarding and service uses; it identifies Malinois as the short-haired fawn black-masked variety.

sources.title: AKC: Belgian Malinois History
sources.evidence: AKC Malinois history reports work on compact Belgian farms moving sheep, goats, geese and ducks without fences, strong human attachment, and later scent detection and police/military roles.

VBO:0200148.summary: Tervuerens often show the Belgian Shepherd’s alert, active confidence and readiness to work closely with people. Descended from the same Belgian herding stock, they retain the quick responses valued for moving flocks and guarding a farm. The variety took its name from Tervuren, where a pair of fawn herding dogs helped establish its early line.
VBO:0200148.historicalRoots: Belgian herding and guarding dog; early Tervuren line associated with the village of Tervuren.

sources.title: FCI: Belgian Shepherd Dog (Standard No. 15)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 15 gives the shared Belgian Shepherd temperament and sheepdog, guarding and service roles; Tervueren is the long-haired fawn or grey black-overlay, black-masked variety.

sources.title: AKC: Belgian Tervuren History
sources.evidence: AKC history names Tom and Poes, a fawn pair in Tervuren, as early ancestors and describes continuing herding, search-and-rescue and dog sport work.

VBO:0200346.summary: Hairless Chinese Cresteds tend to be affectionate, playful companions with an alert streak. Many enjoy a high perch to watch the room, and some turn that lively attention to agility or obedience. Their exposed skin needs protection from cold and strong sun, an extra care need alongside the breed’s cheerful character.
VBO:0200346.historicalRoots: Hairless variety of the Chinese Crested companion dog; precise early geographic origin remains uncertain.

sources.title: FCI: Chinese Crested Dog (Standard No. 288)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 288 recognizes Hairless and Powder Puff varieties, calls the shared breed happy, and notes uncertainty about early origin.

sources.title: AKC: Chinese Crested in Obedience and Sports
sources.evidence: AKC describes Chinese Cresteds as affectionate and playful; its documented hairless obedience dog illustrates sports capacity and says exposed skin needs protection from sun and cold. AKC breed feature identifies high perching as a shared habit.

sources.title: AKC: Facts About the Chinese Crested
sources.evidence: Documents high perching as a shared breed habit, with no coat-variety distinction.

VBO:0201151.summary: Russian Toys are often cheerful, curious companions that keep a close eye on their people. When toy-terrier numbers dwindled in Russia, local breeders revived a distinct line in the 1950s. A longhaired pup born to smooth-coated parents in 1958 helped establish the second coat variety of this devoted little dog.
VBO:0201151.historicalRoots: Russian companion dog revived from local toy-terrier stock in the mid-1950s.

sources.title: FCI: Russian Toy (Standard No. 352)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 352 documents active, cheerful, curious and devoted behavior, Russian 1950s revival, two coat varieties and longhaired emergence from smooth-haired parents.

sources.title: AKC: Russian Toy
sources.evidence: AKC Russian Toy page describes an active cheerful dog fond of staying near human companions.

VBO:0200882.summary: Miniature Bull Terriers tend to greet life with fearless playfulness and a stubborn streak; they can be amusingly determined while remaining people-oriented. Their British line fell so far out of favor that it left the Kennel Club register in 1918, before enthusiasts revived it in 1938.
VBO:0200882.historicalRoots: Smaller British Bull Terrier line revived in 1938 after earlier decline.

sources.title: FCI: Miniature Bull Terrier (Standard No. 359)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 359 describes courageous, fun-loving, sometimes obstinate temperament and records the 1938 Miniature Bull Terrier Club revival after earlier decline.

sources.title: AKC: Miniature Bull Terrier
sources.evidence: AKC characterizes the miniature as upbeat, mischievous and fearless, like the larger Bull Terrier.

VBO:0201258.summary: Smooth Fox Terriers are lively, sociable and quick to meet a new challenge. Britain’s foxhunts shaped a dog ready to pursue foxes, and the old working brief also included rats and rabbits. Their bright, expectant manner hints at a terrier that was bred to move fast and keep its attention on the task.
VBO:0201258.historicalRoots: British foxhunting terrier standardized by the late 19th century.

sources.title: FCI: Smooth Fox Terrier (Standard No. 12)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 12 describes alert, quick, friendly and fearless temperament, British foxhunting roots, and readiness to deal with rats, rabbits and foxes.

sources.title: AKC: Smooth Fox Terrier
sources.evidence: AKC breed page calls the Smooth Fox Terrier lively and gregarious, developed for British foxhunts and closely related to Wire Fox Terriers.

VBO:0200339.summary: Long-haired Chihuahuas are alert, quick to notice a change, and often carry themselves with self-reliant confidence beyond their tiny size. Their lively, courageous character can have a terrier-like air. The breed takes its name from the Mexican state of Chihuahua; images resembling an early type appear at Tula, though the exact ancient lineage remains uncertain.
VBO:0200339.historicalRoots: Mexican companion breed associated with pre-Columbian Techichi imagery; exact lineage uncertain.

sources.title: FCI: Chihuahua (Standard No. 218)
sources.evidence: FCI No. 218 identifies Mexico, quick alert lively courageous temperament, Techichi-like images at Tula, and long-haired/smooth-haired coat varieties; the early descent is framed as an assumption.

sources.title: AKC: Chihuahua
sources.evidence: AKC Chihuahua page identifies an alert, amusing Mexican companion and ancient pre-Columbian associations.

sources.title: Chihuahua Club of America: Official Breed Standard
sources.evidence: The parent club standard describes an alert, confident, self-reliant, terrier-like temperament; applies to both coat varieties.

VBO:0200106.summary: Gentle and affectionate, Auvergne Pointers combine a responsive manner with a strong drive to follow a scent. Hunters in France’s Cantal region shaped the breed over more than two centuries, favoring the endurance needed to work difficult ground.
VBO:0200106.historicalRoots: French pointing dog present in the Cantal region for more than two centuries and shaped for hunting.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 180: Braque d’Auvergne (Auvergne Pointer)
sources.evidence: Present in France’s Cantal region for more than two centuries; created by and for hunters. Gentle, very affectionate, intelligent, obedient, powerful scenting, adapts to family life, with endurance over difficult terrain. Robust square Braque type, black-and-white flecked short coat; undocked tail reaches hock.
